l: Erythræ, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Erythræ was a former city in the Platæan district near Mount Cithæron. Founded by Erythrus, son of Rhadamanthys, it was first associated with settlers from Crete, then occupied by Lycians, Carians, Pamphylians, and other Greeks. Cleopus formed an Ionian colony there. It had temples of Hercules and Athene Polias, Hercules’ wooden raft, and Chalcis, whose sea baths were considered Ionia’s most beneficial.

l: Sarpedon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_bearded bearded [in the painting] Sarpedon is shown beside Memnon, leaning his head on both hands while one of Memnon’s hands rests on his shoulder.

l: Ilium, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Ilium is a city repeatedly defined by its capture. Its fall brings death, escape, and the preservation of Antenor’s household; Æthra reaches the Greek camp, while Eurypylus receives a chest with a statue of Dionysus. Afterward, Agapenor’s Arcadian fleet is driven from its intended return by a storm.

l: Clazomenæ, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Clazomenæ began with no city before the Ionians came to Asia Minor. Ionians from Colophonia built first under Mount Ida, returned to Ionia, and occupied its territory. Most inhabitants came from Cleonæ and Phlius. Fearing the Persians, they moved to the opposite island, which Alexander son of Philip made a peninsula by embankment.

l: Phocæa, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Phocæa, a place, had no city before the Ionians came to Asia Minor. Its people came from Phocis with Philogenes and Damon, gained territory by agreement with Cyme rather than war, then accepted kings from Codrus’s descendants to join the Pan-Ionic confederacy.

l: Mount Ida, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Mount Ida was identified as the region connected with the second Herophile through her mother, one of its Nymphs. The text also describes its thin, porous, red, and very dry soil as the reason the river Aidoneus disappears into the ground.

l: Alexander the son of Philip, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Alexander the son of Philip, a person, built modern Smyrna after a dream on Mount Pagus directed him to relocate Smyrna’s people. He also connected Clazomenæ to the mainland, bribed Chæron to become tyrant of Pellene, made offerings to Æsculapius, and was traditionally said to have died from Styx.

l: Philip, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Philip, son of Demetrius and a Macedonian king, received rule over the Macedonians from his stepfather Antigonus on coming of age. Closely imitating Philip son of Amyntas, he used bribes, poison, including against Aratus of Sicyon, and garrisons to secure power, raiding Athenians and Ætolians. He ended the Phocian or Sacred War, won at Chæronea, restored the Platæans, and stationed a garrison in Thebes to weaken Theban power. He terrorized Elatea and bought influential support. His power later suffered defeat at Cynoscephalæ by Flaminius and the Romans: most of his army was lost, and peace compelled him to remove garrisons from Greek towns seized in war. He was Andriscus's grandfather.

l: Peloponnese, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Peloponnese is a place with coastal states, Corinth, Epidaurus, Trœzen, Hermion, Lacedæmonian territory, Messenia, Sicyon, Achaia, and Elis, and inland Arcadia, which lacks sea access. Its record moves from its divisions and towns to conflicts: Hyllus’s Dorians failed at the Isthmus but later landed near Rhium; an Argive host was destroyed at Ismenius except Adrastus; and Epaminondas aided invited Arcadians, allied with Argives, restored Mantinea, and helped establish Megalopolis.

l: Parnassus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Parnassus is the namesake of Mount Parnassus. After Deucalion’s flood, surviving humans followed wild beasts to its summit; the mountain, sixty stades from Delphi, contains the Corycian cavern, rises above clouds and Ambrosus, and hosts Thyiades’ revels for Dionysus and Apollo.

l: Phocis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Phocis is a region opposite the Peloponnese, near Bœotia and the sea, with ports at Cirrha near Delphi and Anticyra. Its name is linked first to Corinthian Phocus near Tithorea and Delphi, and later to Phocus, son of Æacus, after the crossing of the Æginetans and Phocus. It includes Panopeus, Daulis, Elatea, Abæ, and Stiris, has a Phocian Council, and is approached from Chæronea by roads through Panopeus and Daulis or by rugged Stiris. Its people won against the Thessalians through stratagems and resistance, while it also endured disasters: Oedipus’ pollution at the Cross-roads, towns burned by the Mede, the Phocian War’s effect on Abæ’s temple, and the battle of Delphi, followed by the Galati’s catastrophic retreat and deaths.

l: Pan-Ionic confederacy, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: After Hector and the Chians completed their war against the Abantes and Carians, Hector proposed that he and the Ionians should jointly sacrifice for the welfare of the Pan-Ionic league.

l: colonization of Asia Minor, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The colonization of Asia Minor involved Cretans under Rhacius, captives sent by Apollo, Ionians, and other Greek groups. It produced settlements and cities including Claros, Colophon, Lebedus, Teos, Erythræ, Clazomenæ, and Phocæa.

l: expulsion of the Carians by Mopsus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_carried_out_by Mopsus The expulsion of the Carians by Mopsus followed the settlement of Rhacius and Manto at Claros. Mopsus, their son, drove the Carians out altogether.

l: depopulation of Colophon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_caused_by Lysimachus The depopulation of Colophon was carried out by Lysimachus, as previously described in the account of Lysimachus. The inhabitants were transferred as colonists to Ephesus, where they alone among the colonists fought Lysimachus and the Macedonians.

l: Chios, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Chios is an Ionian city opposite Mimas, associated with Poseidon and rulers Œnopion, Amphiclus, and Hector, and inhabited by Carians and Abantes from Eubœa.

l: Poseidon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Poseidon is a deity associated above all with the sea, horses, riding, temples, oracles, and far-reaching parentage. He fathers Ancæus, Chios, Agelus, Melas, and Œoclus, and is called Pelagæus, Asphalius, and Hippius; Hippius is linked to horses, riding, Arion, and his pursuit of Demeter. He receives horses, was said to have been fed lambs as a child, and has temples, an altar, a statue, worship, and an ancient oracle across many places. He punishes the Achæans with an earthquake after violence against suppliants at Helice, blinds Æpytus with seawater, and reportedly aids the Mantineans in battle. His unions or intrigues include Thyia, Ascra, and Demeter, by whom Despoena is born. In the Eumolpia, he shares the oracle at Delphi with Earth, employs Pyrcon, and later exchanges that oracle for Calauria near Troezen.

l: Procles, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Procles, son of Pityreus and an Epidaurian descended from Ion, led Ionian colonists to Samos and was succeeded there as king by his son Leogorus.

l: Hera, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Hera is a goddess believed by the Samians to have been born on Samos, beside Imbrasus and under a willow-tree in her temple. She is linked with Zeus through intrigue involving Callisto, marriage, estrangement, and reconciliation. As a maiden she was called the Child-goddess, after marriage the Full-grown, and after breaking with Zeus and returning to Stymphelus the Widow. When displeased with Zeus, she went to Eubœa; hearing that he meant to marry Platæa, she tore the clothes from a wooden statue, saw the trick, and reconciled with him. Her worship includes gifts at Helice and Ægæ, temples and statues at several places, and images variously seated, standing, accompanied by Athene and Hebe, or holding Sirens.

l: the temple of Hera in Samos, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The temple of Hera in Samos, dedicated to Hera, was said to be built by Argonauts, with a willow-tree and statue made by Æginetan Smilis.

l: Dædalus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Dædalus is an Athenian of the Metionidæ, son of Palamaon, renowned above all for art and misfortunes. After killing his sister’s son, he voluntarily fled to Crete and stayed at Minos’ court, making works for Minos and his daughters. Credited works include figures of Hercules, Trophonius, Britomartis, Athene, Aphrodite, Ariadne’s dancing-ground, and works later lost or effaced by time. Imprisoned in Crete, he escaped with his son in boats he made, using sails against Minos’ rowed vessels. He went to Sicily, to Cocalus and Inycus, where his art led Cocalus’s daughters to plot against Minos; his fame extended through Sicily and most of Italy.

l: Sicily, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Sicily is a small hill near Athens, but an oracle led Athenians to mistake it for a land beyond their borders, contributing to the fatal war against Syracuse. It also appears in Antiochus the Syracusan’s account of Cnidian colonists, expelled from Pachynus before occupying islands including Lipara, and as the intended destination of an Athenian expedition warned against by prodigies.

l: Italy, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: contains Achæans imprisoned in Etruria [seventeen years after their deportation, only about 300 or fewer remained] The Romans imprisoned the Achæans they had sent to Rome in various towns in Etruria, and 17 years later only about 300 or fewer of the more than 1,000 remained in Italy.

l: Ion the Tragedian, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: recorded Chios (son of Poseidon) [a story of his naming] Ion the Tragedian recorded that Poseidon visited unoccupied Chios, had an intrigue with a Nymph, and named their son Chios because snow fell during the birth. He also recorded the succession of Œnopion and his sons, Amphiclus, and Hector, but did not explain how the Chians came to be ranked as Ionians.

l: Hector, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Hector, son of Priam and king of Chios, fought Abantes and Carians in the war for Chios. After the Chians finished it, he sacrificed to the Pan-Ionic league and received a tripod from the Ionians for prowess. His remains were brought from Ilium to a tomb near the Well of Œdipus, and a painting shows him bearded, sorrowful, and seated.

l: Ionian colonization of Samos and Chios, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Ionian colonization of Samos was led by Procles, whose followers included many Epidaurians banished from Epidauria. Chios was later associated with Amphiclus, who came from Histiæa in Eubœa in accordance with an oracle at Delphi, though the text does not state how the Chians were ranked as Ionians.

l: the expulsion and recovery of Samos, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Androclus and the Ephesians defeated Leogorus, drove the Samians from Samos on the pretext that they had plotted with the Carians, and occupied the island. Some expelled Samians settled at Samothrace and others built a fort at Anæa; ten years later, those under Leogorus crossed back to Samos, expelled the Ephesians, and recovered the island.

l: Mount Pagus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_near Smyrna [the site of the modern city] Mount Pagus was the place from which Alexander the son of Philip returned while hunting before visiting the temple of Nemesis. Modern Smyrna was built on its site or in its vicinity.

l: Nemesis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Nemesis is a goddess, worshiped as two goddesses by Smyrna and linked by differing parentage to Night or Oceanus. She appears with another goddess in Alexander's dream, directing him to build a town and move Smyrna's inhabitants.

l: Alexander's dream, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: concerns Mount Pagus [the dream occurred after hunting there] Alexander's dream occurred after he returned from hunting on Mount Pagus and slept beneath a plane-tree growing in the water before the temple of Nemesis. The goddesses of Nemesis appeared in the dream and told him to build a town there and move Smyrna's people from the old city.

l: relocation of Smyrna, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The people of Smyrna consulted the oracle at Claros about relocating from the old city. They willingly moved after receiving the response that those living near Mount Pagus across the sacred Meles would be thrice and four times happy.

l: oracle of Claros, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: prophesies relocation of Smyrna [that settlement near Mount Pagus would be fortunate] The oracle of Claros responded to Smyrna's consultation with a prophecy praising those who would dwell near Mount Pagus across the sacred Meles. The response encouraged the people of Smyrna to relocate.

l: Ionia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Ionia is a praised region of fertile land and healthy air, rich in temples, baths, rivers, groves, caves, and wonders. Its notable places span Ephesus, Miletus, Colophon, Lebedus, Teos, Clazomenæ, Erythræ, Smyrna, Chios, and Samos, culminating in distinguished temples and the beautiful river Meles.

l: Athene, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Athene is a goddess worshipped under several local names and forms, especially at Aliphera, where inhabitants say she was born and reared and where she has a temple, bronze statue, and festival. Accounts also connect her with the river Triton, though the text disputes whether this is the local river near Alalcomenae or one in Libya. She invents contrivances, gathers flowers with Proserpine in an alternative identification, and is called Onga by Thebans, Hippia by Manthurii, and Alea by other Greeks and Peloponnesians. In action, she drove Enceladus's chariot in the battle of gods and giants, tried as Melas to prevent Teuthis from leaving Aulis, was wounded by him, appeased Hercules, defended Elatea, cursed Cylo's party after the destruction of her suppliants, and aided Tegea through Cepheus with a promise and Medusa's lock. Her worship is marked by temples, shrines, altars, festivals, and many statues: standing beside Zeus, in marketplaces and theatres, in groves, and as images of ivory, gold, bronze, stone, and a wounded thigh. These images preserve both her protection and the local stories attached to her.

l: temple of Hercules at Erythræ, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_dedicated_to Hercules The temple of Hercules at Erythræ was admired for its great antiquity and contained a wooden raft associated with the god's voyage from Tyre in Phœnicia. Only Thracian women were allowed to enter it, and the rope made from their hair was still preserved there.

l: Hercules, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Hercules is variously identified as one of the Idæan Dactyli and as having reached Delphi before the son of Amphitryon; Egyptians and Libyans called him Hercules. He was about a cubit high beside Demeter and was made as a brazen statue by Ageladas. Associated with Cerberus, a raft from Tyre to Erythræ, temples, and the Labours, he took Orchomenians’ horses by night, tied them to chariots, and became Hippodetes.

l: wooden raft of Hercules, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: A wooden raft said to sail from Tyre, moor at the promontory called Mid, and reach the Ionian sea; Erythræ and Chios brought it ashore using a rope made from Thracian women’s hair.

l: Phormio, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Phormio, son of Asopichus, was a blind fisherman from Erythræ who dreamed that women’s hair should be made into a rope to drag a raft ashore; afterward he regained sight for life.

l: Thracian women, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Thracian women alone may enter the temple of Hercules at Erythræ. They plot against and, after drinking wine, kill Orpheus because he led their husbands on wanderings; the account links this to men entering battle drunk.

l: Graces, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Graces are a deity worshipped under differing numbers and names. Eteocles and later custom established three; Lacedæmonians had two. Traditions made them daughters of Zeus and Eurynome, or Ægle and Sun, and named them Charis, Pasithea, Euphrosyne, Aglaia, and Thalia.

l: Æsculapius, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Æsculapius is a deity honored through temples, sacred enclosures, and many statues. Accounts differ: the Phœnician tradition makes him Apollo’s son, while a Sidonian identifies him with health-giving air rather than a mortal woman’s child; at Titane his statue was called Health. As a boy, he was said to have been exposed at Thelpusa, found and raised by Autolaus, and nursed by Trygon, whose tomb stood in his temple. Child-form temples and statues preserve this story. His worship extended through sites including Patræ, Ægium, Tithorea, Thelpusa, and near Mysæum, with works attributed to Alcamenes, Parian Scopas, Timocles, and Timarchides.

l: river Meles, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: has cave near the springs of Meles [near its springs] The sacred Meles was named in the oracle of Claros as lying across from Mount Pagus. Near Smyrna, the river Meles was described as exceptionally beautiful.

l: cave near the springs of Meles, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_associated_with Homer [Homer was said to have written there] A cave near the springs of the Meles was said to be the place where Homer wrote his Poems.

l: Ionian temples and wonders, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: are numerous [their wonders are nearly equal to those of Greece altogether] The Ionian temples and wonders included the temple of Ephesian Artemis, unfinished temples of Apollo at Branchidæ and Claros, temples at Samos, Phocæa, Erythræ, and Priene, and numerous baths, rivers, groves, caves, tombs, and sacred sites. They were described as nearly equal to the wonders of Greece as a whole.

l: Dyme, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Dyme was an Achaean town, formerly called Palea, about 30 stades from the Larisus. It alone in Achaia was reduced in war by Philip the son of Demetrius; Sulpicius then permitted his army to plunder it. Augustus assigned it to Patræ. Its notable sacred and commemorative sites included temples or monuments of Athene, the Dindymene Mother, Attes, Sostratus, and Œbotas.

l: Olenus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Olenus was a small Achaean town near the river Pirus; weakened over time, it was abandoned, and its people moved to Piræ and Euryteæ.

l: Pharæ, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Pharæ is a town in Achaia, reckoned with Patræ since the days of Augustus. About 150 stades from Patræ and 70 from the sea near the Pierus, it has a large market-place, Hermes’ well, sacred stones, and a nearby grove of Castor and Pollux. Its founder remains uncertain.

l: Tritea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Tritea is an inland town of Achaia, reckoned with Patræ by Imperial order and about 120 stades from Pharæ. Its chief features are temples of the Greatest Gods and Athene, with clay and stone statues, and sacrifices to Ares and Tritea. Tradition names either Celbidas or Melanippus as founder; Athene’s old statue was said to have gone to Rome.

l: Ægium, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Ægium is an Achaean town, 60 stades by sea from Erineus and about 40 fewer by land, watered by Phœnix and Miganitas and near Selinus. After Helice was destroyed, it occupied Helice’s territory. Its market-place holds temples of Apollo and Artemis, a tomb of Talthybius, and funeral rites in his honour; its sea-shore and precincts contain further temples, statues, and sacred enclosures. Its cults include Ilithyia, Athene, Hera, Dionysus, Aphrodite, Poseidon, Proserpine, Zeus Homagyrius, Pan-Achæan Demeter, Safety, and Æsculapius. It still hosts the Achæans’ general meeting.

l: Cerynea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Cerynea is an Achaean town on a hill above the high-road, possibly named for the river Cerynites. It grew more powerful through an influx of people of Mycenæ and later became notable for its temple of the Eumenides.

l: Bura, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Bura was an Achaean hill town, said to be named for Bura, daughter of Ion and Helice; an earthquake that destroyed Helice devastated it, leaving none of its old temple statues, despite temples to several deities.

l: Ægira, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Ægira, formerly called Hyperesia in Homer, is an Achaean town and seaport whose upper town lies 12 stades from its port; the port is 72 stades from the temple of Hercules Buraicus. Its ancient Apollo temple and temples of Zeus and Artemis, including Artemis the Huntress on the port road, mark its sacred character. It contains statues and cults of many deities, worshipping Celestial Aphrodite most of all. Roads and sea routes connect it to Phelloe and Aristonautæ.

l: Pellene, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Pellene is an Achaean town next to Ægira, the last Achaean place near Sicyon and Argolis, with Aristonautæ as its seaport and Chelydorea as its mountain boundary. Its people traced its name to Pallas, while Argive tradition traced it to Pellen. Built on the level parts of a steep hill, its uninhabited precipitous summit divides it into two sections. On the approach and within the town are sanctuaries of Athene, Artemis the Saviour, Dionysus the Lighter, Apollo Theoxenius, Artemis the archer, Ilithyia, Poseidon, and other sacred places; it also has a market-place conduit, Glyceæ’s drinkable water below the city, and an old gymnasium for youths. Citizenship requires reaching man’s estate. Pellene honors Promachus with two statues, but avoids mention of Chæron, who took Alexander son of Philip’s bribe to become tyrant.

l: Tellis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Tellis, son of Tisamenus and great-grandson of Archilochus, appears as a youth in Charon’s boat.

l: Preugenes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Preugenes, son of Agenor, was a Lacedæmonian leader sharing authority with Achaean rulers. During Dorian rule of Lacedæmon and Argos, he followed a dream and, aided by a trusted slave, took Artemis Limnatis’s statue from Sparta. He was later commemorated by effigy, tomb, and annual rites.

l: Patreus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Patreus, son of Preugenes and grandson of Agenor, forbids Achæan settlement in Anthea and Mesatis; his tomb and golden effigy stand near the market-place, where annual rites honor him with Preugenes.

l: Patræ, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Patræ is a town in Achæan territory, about 80 stades from Pirus and near Glaucus at the river’s mouth. Preugenes and his son Patreus built it from Lacedæmon; after Patreus enlarged walls near Aroe, it developed from Aroe, Anthea, and Mesatis and took his name. Its people allied with the Achæans against the Lacedæmonians, aided the Ætolians against the Galati, endured reverses and poverty, and later gained inhabitants from various towns under Augustus. It received the statue of Laphrian Artemis from Calydon and celebrates Laphria. Its temples, statues, sea grove, oracle well, and devotion to Aphrodite are prominent. By Imperial order it is reckoned with Pharæ and Tritea.

l: Trojan War, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: During Agamemnon’s expedition against Ilium in the Trojan War, the Achæans provided the largest contingent from Greece because they inhabited both Lacedæmon and Argos.

l: Xerxes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Darius’s son, king of the Persians, carried off sacred statues and led an army that burnt Abæ’s temple and Hyampolis.

l: Medes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Those who fell fighting against the Medes are commemorated by a tomb near the entrance to Platæa. The Medes are associated with the Persian invasion and with the spoils that Themistocles brought to Delphi as a proposed offering to Apollo. One explanation for Apollo’s refusal was that Themistocles would later become a suppliant of the Persians, and acceptance might have brought him the undying hatred of the Medes.

l: Thermopylæ, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Thermopylæ is a strategic Greek pass and entry route into Greece, defended by Phocians through the mountain. It hosted Greek forces during the Persian and Galatian invasions. Leonidas fought there without the Achæans in the Persian invasion; later, Greeks gathered there in greater numbers against Brennus and the Galatians. Its narrow, smooth, rocky ground and streams hindered cavalry and helped cause Galatian losses. When Brennus crossed Mount Œta to the Greek rear, Athenians evacuated troops by triremes and the contingents dispersed.

l: Themistocles, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Themistocles, child of Neocles, is honored at Olympia after expelling Xerxes from Greece by sea-fights. He brings Median spoils to Apollo, but the priestess rejects them, a refusal linked to his later supplication to the Persians.

l: Platæa, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Platæa is a town reached from Eleutheræ, ruled by Cithæron and bounded from Thebes by the Asopus. Near its entrance are tombs of fighters against the Medes, a trophy, and Zeus Eleutherius’s altar, statue, and Eleutheria festival. Within are hero-chapels and temples. It is presented as Asopus’s daughter in Zeus’s deception of Hera, whose reconciliation the festival commemorates, and contains Gargaphia and Leitus’s tomb.

l: Zeus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Zeus is a deity worshiped under several names and represented by statues, altars, precincts, temples, and an oracle. At Dodona, he warns the Athenians about the Areopagus and the smoking altars of the Eumenides and orders protection for defeated Lacedæmonians as suppliants. As Zeus Lycæus, he is linked to Lycaon, the Lycæa, Mount Lycæus, secret sacrifices, and rites during drought; Arcadians and Methydrium people place his birth or rearing there. He has precincts and a stone temple at Megalopolis, while Zeus Eleutherius has an altar and white-stone statue at Platæa. His actions include an intrigue with Callisto, ordering Hermes to save her child and making that child the Great Bear; sending the Fates to grieving Demeter; and using a dressed wooden statue and a proposed marriage to Platæa to reconcile Hera. He is also called Lecheates, is father of Dionysus through Semele, and receives a sceptre from Hephæstus.

l: Olympia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Olympia is a place of Olympian games, victories, and honors. When Hercules the Theban established the games, Iasius reportedly won the horserace and victors received wild-olive crowns. After Iphitus restored the games, Corœbus was first victor; Damaretus first won the heavy-armour race; Arrhachion won twice before the 54th. It also held Œbotas’s statue, honored by competitors and victors.

l: Greece, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Greece is a country containing Megalopolis, rich in silver, gold, and temple offerings, and important enough to serve as a comparison with distant Libya, India, and Arabia. Its history is presented as a movement between freedom, external threat, internal betrayal, and Roman control. It was invaded by Xerxes and the Medes, while the Achæans stood apart from the principal Greek forces; after the Galati crossed into Asia Minor, no Greek state was clearly preeminent. Philip threatened it through garrisons and raids. Greece was weak when Brennus and the Galati targeted its wealth, but the expedition that reached Delphi ended in the invaders’ ruin. Greece later achieved autonomy and freedom through the arms of Thebes and the deeds associated with Epaminondas, after having been nearly ruined by leaders of the Peloponnesian War and partly recovering through Conon and Epaminondas. It was freed by Titus Flaminius, yet treason repeatedly destroyed its cities more than plague had done. After Rome defeated Perseus, Greece became subject to Rome: taxes, restrictions, and the suppression of national meetings followed, though the meetings, cross-border landholding, and remission of fines were later restored. Philopœmen warned that submission to Rome hastened Greece’s fate; he was its last public benefactor, after Miltiades. Nero made Greece entirely free, but discord under Vespasian brought taxes and obedience to a Roman prætor. Greece is ultimately described as extremely weak, having ceased to produce distinguished men, and later was overrun by the Costoboci.

l: Chæronea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Chæronea is a town, formerly called Arne and, by local tradition, named for Chæron, son of Apollo and Thero. It is remembered for battles: the Thebans fell against Philip nearby, Sulla and the Romans raised two trophies there, and Metellus and the Romans cut down returning Arcadians. It makes flower-boiled unguents, lies below the crag Petrachos, and begins routes into Phocis, including roads toward Delphi and Stiris.

l: Lamia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_a battle site [where the Greeks suffered a reverse] After the reverse to the Greeks at Lamia, Antipater wanted to cross quickly to the war in Asia Minor and was willing to make a rapid peace. At Lamia, although only 200 Greeks fell, the Athenians became slaves of the Macedonians.

l: Galati, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Galati were a barbarian Celtic army and migrating force that moved from Europe toward Asia, crossing the Hellespont and later entering Asia Minor by ships. They repeatedly campaigned toward Greece, initially retreating from Thrace as too few, then returning in greater strength under divided commanders against several peoples. Their forces included 152,000 infantry and 20,400 horse; each horse-soldier had two mounted servants who could replace casualties, making the actual cavalry count 61,200. They were marked by desperate valour, cruelty, limited skill in war, and shields as their only defensive armour. They plundered the treasures at Delphi, ravaged near Heraclea, killed people in the fields, and attempted temple plunder, but failed to take Heraclea and suffered defeats at Thermopylæ and Mount Œta. A 40,800-man expedition devastated Callion, for which the Ætolians fined them; Brennus also led 40,000 picked Galati against the Phocians. They did not habitually mourn or seek burial for their dead. Prophecy portrayed their crossing into Asia, destruction of cities, and eventual destruction by Attalus. In Pessinus, they avoided pork.

l: Peloponnesians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Peloponnesians, including the Achæans, came to Athens under Codrus but mostly withdrew from Attica after his death. They used the title Alea for Athene, later failed to guard Thermopylæ against the Galati, and, with other Greek allies, supplied war money for the Athenian portico.

l: Leuctra, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Leuctra is a place in Bœotia. It was home to Scedasus, whose memory Epaminondas honored there while vowing a battle. The Thebans and Lacedæmonians fought at Leuctra; the Lacedæmonians were then shut up there. Oracles foretold the lamentable battle, and its reverse preceded Megalopolis’s colonization.

l: Arcadians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Arcadians are a people or nation whose inhabitants were called Pelasgi before Arcas’s reign, when they became Arcadians. Under Arcas they learned agriculture, breadmaking, weaving, and spinning; they were later ruled by Echemus, Agapenor, and other kings. They preserve a very old tradition of wolf transformation and maintain local sacred accounts: Mount Lycæus is Olympus or the Sacred Hill, and its Cretea, not the island of Crete, was where Zeus was reared. They associate Arne with a lamb, connect Mantinea’s river Ophis with Antinoe’s serpent guide, place the giants’ battle with the gods at Bathos, and sacrifice there to thunder, lightning, and storms. Their strongest religious distinction is worship of Despœna above all gods. They perform her Mystic rites, exclude pomegranate wood from her temple, and sacrifice animals by cutting off whichever limb a worshipper first touches. Their history is marked by shifting warfare and alliances. They fought at Ilium, supported Messenia and Aristodemus against the Lacedæmonians, and punished two men named Aristocrates by stoning: one for defiling Artemis Hymnia’s sanctuary and one for bribery and betrayal of the Messenians. They fought at Platæa, at times served the Lacedæmonians against the Athenians under compulsion, joined Agesilaus in Asia Minor, and fought at Leuctra. After the Lacedæmonian reverse there, they joined the Thebans, though they later stayed neutral against Philip and the Macedonians, Antipater, and the Galati. They became especially zealous members of the Achæan League. Most supported Antony at Actium, while Mantineans supported Augustus. They accompanied Evander from Pallantium in a colony near the Tiber. In the Peloponnese, they invited Epaminondas, evacuated insecure small towns, and inhabited the new Megalopolis. Finally, about a thousand picked men who had fought with Critolaus went to Elatea and were received through old kinship, but Romans met and cut them to pieces at Chæronea, presented as punishment for their earlier abandonment of Greeks fighting Philip and the Macedonians.

l: Megalopolis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Megalopolis is a city and large town in Arcadia, Greece, created as one large settlement for Arcadians gathered from many towns after Epaminondas the Theban persuaded them to leave insecure small towns. Epaminondas is regarded as its founder, alongside founders from Mantinea, Tegea, Clitor, Mænalus, and Parrhasium. Peopled zealously by Arcadians, it received Greece’s best wishes and became strong through alliance with Thebes, whose arms crowned it. It resisted Lacedæmonian attacks, defeated Acrotatus and, under Aristodemus, the Lacedæmonians; its Myropolis portico was built from Lacedæmonian spoils. It later joined the Achæan League. Cleomenes eventually captured and destroyed it by fire, defeating and expelling its people; a nearby monument to those killed in that battle was called the Treaty Violation because he violated the treaty. During this crisis Philopœmen, a native, evacuated two-thirds of the adult citizens and all women and children to Messene, then brought exiles back armed without accepting conditions. Pylades, a Pythian-winning harper, was also native to the city. The Helisson divides Megalopolis into two parts; the southern side contains a theatre. It had a market-place, temples, precincts, porticoes, public offices, and a council chamber, as well as the Philip’s portico and a statue honoring Polybius. It borders Heræa at the sources of the Buphagus, and the Alpheus reemerges at Pegæ in its territory. Roads lead from it toward Messene, Lacedæmon, Methydrium, Pallantium, Tegea, and other inland places, including through its suburb Ladocea. Once prestigious and fortunate, it had, in the author’s day, lost that standing and become mostly ruins.

l: Messenians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Messenians, bordering Lacedæmon, were restored by Epaminondas, the Thebans, and Argives, and helped the Thebans during Thebes’s restoration. Later, divided between wealthy and popular parties, they captured the wounded Philopœmen; Dinocrates and the wealthy urged execution while the popular party sought to save him.

l: Alexander, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Alexander, Roxana’s son and a ruler in Thessaly, is associated with early death, victories over Darius and in India without trophies, hostility toward Thebes, and actions against Antipater. Though friendly to Pelopidas and the Thebans, he treacherously imprisoned Pelopidas; when Epaminondas approached with a Theban force, he lost confidence and released him. Cassander later sought to destroy Alexander’s house.

l: Cassander, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Cassander, married to Thessalonica, was driven by hatred of Alexander: he opposed Alexander’s house, restored Thebes, ordered Olympias stoned, and poisoned Alexander’s sons Hercules and Alexander. He led Macedonians in the ineffective blockade of Elatea, then died of dropsy and worms; his sons later died violently or prematurely.

l: wars of the Achæans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Achæans fought in Agamemnon’s expedition against Ilium, later allied with Patræ and the Athenians against the Lacedæmonians, and fought at Chæronea against Philip and the Macedonians. They did not join the battles at Thermopylæ, Salamis, or Platæa during Xerxes’ invasion, and they did not fight at Lamia.

l: Persian invasion of Greece, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Persian invasion of Greece brought a barbarian landing at Marathon and Xerxes’ advance. Miltiades checked the Persian host; Greek forces under Leonidas gathered at Thermopylæ, though the Achæans stayed home. Leonidas fought there, while Themistocles and the Athenians fought at Salamis; Themistocles’ two sea-fights expelled Xerxes, followed by allied action at Platæa.

l: Galatian migration into Asia Minor, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: occurs_during Athenian archonship of Democles [the following year] The Galatian migration into Asia Minor began when the Galati crossed over in ships after the pass at Thermopylæ had been left unguarded. Their arrival coincided with the weakening of the principal Greek states and the absence of a clearly leading power in Greece.

l: war between the Peloponnesians and the Athenians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: During the war between the Lacedæmonians and Athenians, the Achæans readily allied themselves with the people of Patræ and were equally friendly with the Athenians.

l: Achæan League, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Achæan League was a Greek political league, formed by common consent at Ægium. The Sicyonians were its first non-Achæan members; other Peloponnesians joined, and increasing power drew Greeks from outside the Isthmus. Its membership came to include Corinth, Argos, the Lacedæmonians, Heraclea under Mount Œta, Orchomenus, Mantineans, Megalopolis, and other Greek cities. Some cities entered amid conflict: Mantineans joined after breaking with the Lacedæmonians, fought with an Achæan force under Aratus, and later helped weaken Lacedæmonian power; Megalopolis joined and honored Lydiades. Philopœmen compelled the Lacedæmonians to join, and the League treated them severely, including requiring their youths to train in the Achæan manner. It exercised jurisdiction over them except in capital cases and resisted member cities' attempts to send private embassies to Rome without common consent. Rome increasingly shaped its affairs: a Roman Senator addressed a general meeting; capital cases were assigned to foreign, meaning Roman, courts; Gallus could release towns; and the Senate ruled that several incorporated cities lacked ancestral connection with the Achæans and should not be compelled to remain. Metellus ordered those cities, including the Lacedæmonians, to leave. Diophanes was chosen general, and the League was described as the organization into which he first ranged all the Peloponnese; its member cities later received Roman permission for Polybius to establish constitutions and frame laws.

l: Sicyonians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Sicyonians planned to invade Hyperesia but withdrew after mistaking goat-borne torches for allied campfires; they later destroyed Donussa and have an empty treasury at Delphi.

l: Agis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Agis, king of Sparta and son of Eudamidas, attacked Megalopolis with a larger, better-equipped army, commanded the Lacedæmonians, then was surrounded and fell in battle.

l: Aratus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Aratus, a benefactor of all Greece discussed in Sicyon, commands Sicyonians and Achæans, helps drive Agis from Pellene, then suffers defeat by Cleomenes at Dyme.

l: Cleomenes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Cleomenes, son of Leonidas and king of the other Spartan royal family, is portrayed as a ruler who replaced the kingdom with his own autocracy. He captured Megalopolis in peacetime, killed captives, destroyed and burned the city, and later offered its people return under a treaty. He also made peace with the Achæans alongside Antigonus.

l: Antigonus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Antigonus rules Macedonians as regent for Philip, his uncle and stepfather; makes peace with Cleomenes and Achæans, defeats Lacedæmonians with Achæans at Sellasia, and surrenders rule when Philip comes of age.

l: Arcadia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Arcadia is an inland, interior division of the Peloponnese, entirely shut off from the sea. Near Argolis it is inhabited by Tegea, Mantinea, and other Arcadians, and it is entered through passes toward Tegea and Mantinea. Roads connect Mantinea with other parts and lead into the interior; the region contains towns, rivers, temples, ruins, Melangea, Pallantium, Heræa, and land near Schœnus. Its people and places are linked by traditions: Pelasgus first settled the land, which was called Pelasgia during his reign and before Arcas; in the third generation after Pelasgus it increased in population and cities, many founded by Lycaon’s sons. Under Arcas it became Arcadia. After Clitor died childless, the kingdom passed to Æpytus, son of Elatus, and later to Aleus. Arcadians went to Troy in transports provided by Agamemnon, fought the Lacedæmonians with each town under its own commander, and later crowded into Megalopolis for strength against them, despite resistance from several towns and the departure of Trapezus’ people from the Peloponnese. Pallantium sent Evander and Arcadians to establish a colony near the river Tiber. Arcadia also figures in accounts of Pan, Leto, and a common altar maintained by Tegea for all Arcadians.

l: Sellasia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Sellasia was the site of a battle in which Philopœmen fought against Cleomenes and the Lacedæmonians. The forces opposing Cleomenes included the Achæans, Arcadians from all the cities, and Antigonus with an army from Macedonia.

l: Philip the son of Amyntas, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Philip, son of Amyntas, is a Macedonian king regarded as the most valiant among Macedonian kings, yet judged not good because he breaks oaths to the gods, violates truces, and dishonours good faith. He joins the Thebans in the war against the Phocians, defeats them, and his victory brings Onomarchus’s flight and death. He later encamps at Nestane and seeks, through Arcadia, to detach the Arcadians from the other Greeks. During his reign many Greek cities are betrayed. After Chaeronea he removes Linus’s remains in obedience to a dream, but erects no trophies for any victory.

l: Corinth, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Corinth is a strongly fortified garrison-town in the Peloponnese. Occupied by Philip’s Macedonian garrison and besieged by Flaminius, it joined the Achæan League after the garrison was overcome. Though the Senate said it should not be forced into that League, it became an Achæan military center. After battle it was left open; Mummius entered, burned it, killed inhabitants, sold captives, removed valuables, and destroyed its walls.

l: Ætolia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Ætolia, inhabited by Ætolians, faced war with the Galati: after Callion’s destruction, its people returned from Thermopylæ to defend remaining towns. Later Augustus depopulated it to populate Nicopolis near Actium.

l: Ætolians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Ætolians were a group inhabiting Pleuron, active in war, alliances, commemoration, and later migration. They sought release from the Achæan League, aided the men of Elis through kinship, protected Heraclea, and suborned an assassin against Nabis. After subduing the Acarnanians, they displayed effigies of their generals, Apollo, and Artemis; they also dedicated shields, a trophy, and a statue of Ætolia from a fine imposed on the Galati. Harassed by Philip’s raids, they received nominal Roman help but were later opposed by Romans and Achæans. Their most prominent action was resisting the Galati: people of every age and women joined, harrying the retreat with missiles, attacking Acichorius’ troops, and helping prevent most Galati from returning. After Augustus removed many to Nicopolis, many migrated to Amphissa.

l: Romans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Romans are a people of Rome and a western power, allied with the Achæans, whose record centers on military intervention and political control in Greece and Macedonia. They first sent soldiers ostensibly to aid the Ætolians against Philip while observing Macedonian aims, then dispatched an army under Otilius to protect Athenians and Ætolians; their Senate replaced him after his unauthorized destruction of Hestiæa and Anticyra. They defeated Philip and Macedonian supremacy, fought the Ætolians and Antiochus, compelled the withdrawal of Macedonian garrisons, and later sent Titus Flaminius to free all Greece, invite Elatea to leave the Macedonians, and grant Elateans freedom and immunity. Their alliance with the Achæans deteriorated as they repeatedly intervened between the Achæans and Lacedæmonians, restored Lacedæmonian exiles and national training, and empowered Gallus to arbitrate and release towns from the Achæan League. After defeating Perseus and the Macedonian Empire, they arranged Macedonia for Roman interests, summoned accused Achæans to Rome, imprisoned them in Etruria without prior conviction, and largely ignored embassies and supplications. They later ended the war against Andriscus under Metellus and ordered the Achæans not to attack Sparta. The conflict culminated in a Roman vote condemning the Achæans for treason and the dispatch of Mummius with naval and land forces. After victories at Chæronea and over the Achæans, Romans killed many in Corinth, enslaved women, children, and other captives, removed valuable offerings and ornaments to Rome, and imposed restrictions on Greece, though they later restored some institutions and remitted fines. Elsewhere they fought Nabis with a fleet, granted him a truce, defeated Antiochus and the Syrians at Thermopylæ, and erected a Chæronea trophy for victory over Taxilus and Mithridates' army.

l: Rome, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Rome begins as land near the Tiber, inhabited by Evander and Arcadians who accompanied him, later becoming part of Rome. It becomes a center of Roman authority: it allies with the Athenians, sends forces against Philip, and receives Achæans ordered there for trial, many of whom are treated as condemned and imprisoned in Etrurian towns. Appeals, embassies, disputes, fines, and arbitration involving the Oropians, Ætolians, Lacedæmonians, Achæans, and Athenians are brought before Rome and its Senate. Rome then sends envoys, Mummius, and advisers to settle disputes and direct war against the Achæans; it receives Corinthian offerings, restores institutions, remits fines, and governs Greece through a prætor. Finally, wars involving Rome include Antonine's victories over Germans and Sauromatae.

l: Roman Otilius, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Roman Otilius, a Roman commander, was ordered to protect Athenians and Ætolians against Philip. He otherwise obeyed, but captured and razed Hestiæa and Anticyra despite their necessary submission to Philip, then was superseded by Flaminius.

l: Flaminius, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Titus Flaminius, a Roman general sent by Rome to free all Greece, urged Elatea to revolt and promised its ancient polity, defeated Macedonians at Eretria and Cynoscephalae, plundered Eretria, besieged Corinth, urged Achaeans to join Romans, and pursued Hannibal alive.

l: Roman Senate, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Roman Senate is an institution that receives accusations, issues orders, appoints representatives, and determines disputes involving the Achæans, Lacedæmonians, Athenians, and other communities. It first supersedes Otilius after the destruction of Hestiæa and Anticyra, then hears accusations against the Achæans from Areus, Alcibiades, and Metellus. It appoints Appius and later Roman ambassadors to mediate or arbitrate between the Lacedæmonians and Achæans, while ordering Athens and Ætolia to restore Messenian and Achæan exiles to their rights. Its decisions favor limits on compulsory membership in the Achæan League: it holds that the Lacedæmonians, Argos, Heraclea under Mount Œta, and Orchomenus should not be forced into it; the chapter record also includes Corinth. It authorizes Gallus to release towns from the League, directs Sicyon to fine Athens for harm to Oropians, then reduces that fine from 500 to 100 talents. It also directs the Lacedæmonians to try non-capital cases before the Achæan League.

l: Anticyra, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Anticyra, formerly Cyparissus and named for Anticyreus, was an ancient town below Medeon, renowned for hellebore on rocky hills. Its people were expelled first by Philip son of Amyntas and later by the Roman Otilius for backing Philip son of Demetrius; after being taken, it was razed. It had market-place statues, Poseidon’s temple, two gymnasiums, a conduit, and a tomb, and lay about 100 stades from Bulis amid uncertain mountain-road access.

l: Achæan League formation, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: occurred_at Ægium The Achæan League was formed at Ægium because the town had been prominent in Achaia and was then its most powerful town, following Helice's destruction by a flood. The Sicyonians joined first, and other Peloponnesians followed immediately or later.

l: battle against Cleomenes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The battle against Cleomenes involved Achæans and Cleomenes, followed Cleomenes' treaty violation, and is commemorated by a roadside monument.

l: capture and destruction of Megalopolis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The capture and destruction of Megalopolis was carried out by Cleomenes, who seized the city in peace, killed Lydiades and captives, expelled defenders, razed and burned it; Philopœmen led survivors to Messenia.

l: battle of Sellasia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The battle of Sellasia was fought at Sellasia between Cleomenes and the Lacedæmonians and the Achæans, Arcadians, Antigonus, and a Macedonian army. Philopœmen joined the infantry, fought courageously, and was wounded in both thighs. The battle ended in the defeat of Cleomenes and the Lacedæmonians and an Achæan victory.

l: Philip's accession to rule over the Macedonians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: transferred_rule_to Philip, the son of Demetrius [from Antigonus when Philip came of age] Philip, the son of Demetrius, took rule over the Macedonians from his stepfather Antigonus when he came of age. Antigonus was willing to surrender the rule, while Philip soon caused fear among the Greeks through his methods and military policies.

l: Roman military intervention against Philip, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Romans first sent soldiers to assist the Ætolians nominally while investigating Macedonian intentions, then sent an army under Otilius to protect the Athenians and Ætolians against Philip. Otilius's destruction of Hestiæa and Anticyra displeased the Roman Senate, which replaced him with Flaminius.

l: Nabis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Nabis was a tyrant of Lacedæmon, described as a man of extreme, unrelenting cruelty. He first attacked the Messenians, took all Messene but its citadel, and withdrew when Philopœmen arrived. He later fought the Romans and gained a temporary truce. A Calydonian, suborned by the Ætolians, assassinated him; his power at Sparta ended.

l: Lycurgus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Lycurgus succeeds Aleus as king as eldest son, kills Areithous by guile, has sons Epochus and Ancæus, and lives to advanced old age after surviving both sons.

l: Metellus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Metellus is a Roman commander whose actions shape Rome’s conflict with the Achæans and campaigns in Macedonia. He and colleagues first urge kinder treatment of the Lacedæmonians; after the Achæans refuse without a Senate decree, he returns to Rome and reports against them, including untrue claims. He leads the Roman army against Andriscus in Macedonia, ends that war quickly, and orders envoys to restrain Achæan war against Sparta. He later proclaims terms inviting cities to leave the Achæan League, defeats opposing forces, occupies Thebes and Megara, protects Thebes, and offers peace and harmony before being sent to Macedonia after Mummius takes command.

l: Thessalians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Thessalians are a Greek group represented in the general Council of the Greeks and by six Amphictyonic Council members. They consult Delphi about Ceressus and make offerings there. As persistent neighbors and enemies of the Phocians, they attack at Hyampolis, invade with forces from all cities, kill Gelon and 300 men, but suffer repeated defeats, including against Phocian cavalry and a night attack.

l: Macedonian supremacy, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Macedonian supremacy unfolds from an end linked to Alexander’s early death in the author’s reflection, through later Philip’s defeat at Cynoscephalæ, to overthrow by the Romans with Perseus. Its collapse is presented as a fatal Roman blow and as the beginning of troubles leading to Achæan subjection to Rome.

l: battle of Cynoscephalæ, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: At the battle of Cynoscephalæ, Philip fought Flaminius and the Romans and was badly defeated. He lost most of his army and was forced to accept terms requiring the removal of his garrisons from Greek towns.

l: Cynoscephalæ, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Cynoscephalæ was the range of hills where Philip and the Macedonians were defeated by Flaminius and the Romans.

l: Roman-Macedonian peace, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_obtained_by Philip [through entreaties and great expenditure of money] The peace obtained by Philip from the Romans sounded impressive but was secured through entreaties and great expenditure of money. Its terms required him to remove his garrisons from the Greek towns he had seized and reduced during the war.

l: Sibyl, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Sibyl, the first Herophile, is an extremely ancient woman and first chanter of oracles. Said by Greeks to be daughter of Zeus and Lamia and called Sibyl by Libyans, she foretells Macedonian power’s rise and fall under the first and last Philip.

l: Attalus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Attalus, king of Pergamus from the East, cooperates with Romans, commands troops under Philopœmen, and is foretold as a bull-horned helper bringing destruction to the Galati.

l: Roman capture and destruction of Corinth, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: A Roman military operation in which Flaminius besieged Corinth after defeating the Macedonian garrison at Eretria; the Achæans joined and Corinth entered their League. Later Mummius entered the open city, burned it, killed many inhabitants, enslaved survivors, and seized valuables.

l: Roman expedition against Macedonia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_finished_by Romans [with the greatest despatch] The Romans, supported by the Achæans, fought against Philip and the Macedonians. Their victory at Cynoscephalæ dealt a fatal blow to Macedonian supremacy and forced Philip to withdraw his garrisons from the Greek towns.

l: Areus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Areus, a prominent Spartan exiled by Nabis, was received and restored by the Achæans despite Lacedæmonian opposition; afterward he denounced them before the Roman Senate, joined Appius’ suite, and was declared guiltless by Appius’ delegation.

l: Alcibiades, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: opposes Achæans [despite having been received and restored by them] Alcibiades had been exiled by Nabis and received and restored by the Achæans. He later denounced the Achæans before the Roman Senate, accompanied Appius, and was declared by Appius’ delegation to have committed no crime against them.

l: Appius, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: favors Lacedæmonians [and consistently opposes the Achæans] Appius was sent by the Roman Senate to settle the differences between the Achæans and Lacedæmonians. He and his suite provoked the Achæans, supported Areus and Alcibiades, favored the Lacedæmonians, and secured decisions restoring exiles and remitting fines.

l: Lycortas, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Lycortas, an Arcadian second to none in merit and friend of Philopœmen, was an Achæan general. He defended Achæan claims before the council while covertly criticizing the Romans, then led Arcadian and Achæan forces against Messenia; its popular party joined him, and Philopœmen’s murderers were executed.

l: Philopœmen, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Philopœmen, son of Craugis, was an Arcadian warrior, Achæan general, cavalry leader, and ultimately celebrated public benefactor of Greece. Raised under Cleander after his father’s death, he was exceptionally strong though not handsome, farmed his own land, hunted, and studied sophists and military strategy. He modeled his aims on Epaminondas but was hot-tempered and avoided athletic competition. When Cleomenes captured Megalopolis, Philopœmen led roughly two-thirds of its lads and grown men, along with its women and children, safely to Messene. He resisted an unarmed return, fought in the cavalry at Sellasia despite spear wounds through both thighs, then served as a mercenary captain in Crete. Returning home, he became commander of the Achæan cavalry and made it the best in Greece, defeating enemy cavalry and killing Demophantus. As Achæan commander in chief and later general again, he reformed the infantry’s arms and equipment, commanded at Mantinea, defeated the Lacedæmonians and slew Machanidas, defended Megara, opposed Nabis, and repeatedly aided the Gortynians in Crete. He compelled the Lacedæmonians to join the Achæan League, acted forcefully at Sparta, reorganized it through exile, sale of Helots, demolition of walls, and altered youth training, and opposed concessions to the Romans. Honoured highly by Greeks, he was remembered as wise in counsel, brave in the field, above money, victorious over two Spartan tyrants, and an abolisher of slavery. In old age, feverish and over seventy, he went with Lycortas into Messenia, was wounded, captured, and killed by poison on Dinocrates’ orders; his remains were returned to Megalopolis.

l: Roman embassy to the Achæans and Lacedæmonians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The embassy led by Appius was sent to place the differences between the Achæans and Lacedæmonians on a just footing. Its members supported the Lacedæmonians, restored exiles, remitted fines of people condemned in their absence, and authorized Lacedæmonian envoys to go to Rome.

l: murder of Philopœmen, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The murder of Philopœmen was carried out by Dinocrates and accomplices through poison. Afterward, the Achæans were thought to banish involved Messenians; Lycortas marched against Messenia, accomplices were executed, and Dinocrates committed suicide.

l: differences between the Achæans and Lacedæmonians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_settled_by Roman embassy to the Achæans and Lacedæmonians [under Roman plenipotentiary authority] The differences concerned the treatment and status of the Lacedæmonians within the Achæan League, the return of exiles, fines, and judicial authority. Roman interventions settled these matters in ways that the Achæans regarded as unjust and increasingly favorable to the Lacedæmonians.

l: restoration of exiles and remission of fines, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_ordered_by Romans [as part of the settlement imposed on the Achæans and Lacedæmonians] Appius and his fellow plenipotentiaries restored to Sparta those exiled by the Achæans and remitted the fines of people who had fled before judgment and been condemned in their absence. The restored Lacedæmonians then promoted appeals by Messenian and Achæan exiles, and the Roman Senate ordered their restoration to their rights.

l: betrayal of one’s country and fellow citizens for gain, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: A crime deemed most impious, betrayal for gain repeatedly troubles and weakens Greece, illustrated through cases involving Samians, Eretria, Thessaly, Thebes, Elis, and others.

l: Persians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Persians were defeated in the actions at Artemisium and Salamis, and their spoils were brought as possible offerings to Apollo. The invasion by the Persians was said to have been foretold in the oracles of Bacis and in the earlier verses of Euclus.

l: Peloponnesian war, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Peloponnesian War nearly ruined Greece through the actions of its renowned figures, including the Lacedæmonians’ siege and capture of Platæa.

l: Lysander, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Lysander, a Lacedæmonian and son of Aristocritus, commanded the Peloponnesian fleet, gained Cyrus’s money, defeated Antiochus, and captured 100 Athenian ships at Ægos-potamoi. He condemned Eteonicus for injustice but executed Philocles and 4000 Athenian captives without burial. He established Decemvirates and Harmosts, encouraged love of money, and was judged to harm the Lacedæmonians. Crowned by Poseidon at Delphi, he fell attacking Haliartus.

l: Antipater, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Antipater, after the Greek reverse at Lamia, initially makes speedy peace with Athens and leaves Greece free to pursue war in Asia Minor. Persuaded by Demades and other Athenian traitors, he changes course; he also kills his mother Thessalonice for favoring Alexander.

l: Perseus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Perseus, king of Macedonia and father of Andriscus, began at peace with the Romans under Philip's agreement, but attacked their ally Abrupolis and dispossessed the Sapæans, violating the peace and leading Macedonia to defeat in war.

l: Roman Senators, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Ten Roman Senators, sent after Perseus and the Macedonians were defeated, settled Macedonian affairs; one, influenced by Callicrates, urged accusations against alleged supporters and sent them to Rome.

l: Callicrates, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Callicrates was an Achæan general and traitor to the Achæan cause who gained influence over the Achæans through friendship with the Romans and flattery of Roman Senators. He accused prominent Achæans and generals of favoring Perseus and the Macedonians, helping send more than 1,000 Achæans to Rome, and was called the plague of all Greece. After assisting the Oropians, he prosecuted Menalcidas when denied promised money. Sent with Diæus to Rome against the Spartan exiles, he died of illness on the road.

l: Amphictyonic Council, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Amphictyonic Council, held at Thermopylæ and Delphi, punished temple plunderers and fined the Phocians. After the Sacred War it admitted Macedonians, gave them the Phocian votes, and excluded Phocians and Lacedæmonians; the Phocians were later restored for bravery against Brennus. Augustus transferred several votes to Nicopolis. In the author’s time it had thirty members, with Athens, Delphi, and Nicopolis represented at every meeting.

l: overthrow of Perseus and the Macedonian Empire by the Romans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: begins troubles of the Achæans The overthrow of Perseus and the Macedonian Empire by the Romans is identified as the beginning of the Achæans’ troubles. It was followed by Roman intervention in Macedonia and the eventual subjection of the Achæans.

l: war between Perseus and the Romans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_caused_by Perseus the son of Philip [following the outrage against the Sapæans] The war began after Perseus violated his peace agreement with the Romans by attacking Abrupolis, king of the Sapæans, who were Roman allies. Perseus and the Macedonians were defeated because of this outrage.

l: trial of the Achæans at Rome, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_ordered_by Roman Senators [after accusations by Callicrates] The trial of the Achæans at Rome followed accusations by Callicrates and a Roman Senator that prominent Achæans had supported Perseus. More than 1,000 Achæans were sent to Rome, despite the earlier objection that they should not be condemned before their alleged actions were identified.

l: Achæans imprisoned in Etruria, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: More than 1,000 Achæans, held in various towns in Etruria and treated as condemned, were ignored despite repeated embassies and supplications; seventeen years later Romans released about 300 or fewer surviving prisoners as sufficiently punished.

l: Gallus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Gallus, a Roman Senator, is sent to Greece to arbitrate Lacedæmonian-Argive disputes. He treats Greeks, especially both parties, with extreme contempt and is empowered to release as many towns as he wishes from the Achæan League.

l: disputes between the Lacedæmonians and the Argives, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Disputes between the Lacedæmonians and Argives were submitted to Philip and Callicrates, then Gallus rejected arbitration contemptuously.

l: Oropus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_subject_to Athenians Oropus was a town subject to the Athenians. The Athenians plundered it twice, and an Athenian garrison occupied it for a time before withdrawing.

l: Oropians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Oropians appealed to the Roman Senate after Athenians plundered Oropus. Though they accepted an arrangement with an Athenian garrison and hostages, an outrage led them to demand both hostages’ return and the garrison’s removal. They promised Menalcidas ten talents for Achaean assistance, then paid despite receiving none.

l: plundering of Oropus by the Athenians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_caused_by war with the Macedonians [through Athenian poverty] The Athenians first plundered Oropus out of necessity rather than choice because of their poverty. After the Achaean army was summoned to help the Oropians, the Athenians returned, plundered what they had spared in their first raid, and withdrew their garrison.

l: fine imposed on the Athenians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: amounts_to 500 talents [imposed in their absence by the Sicyonians] The Sicyonians fined the Athenians 500 talents in their absence for the harm done to the Oropians. The Roman Senate remitted all but 100 talents, and the Athenians did not pay the remaining amount.

l: Athenian garrison at Oropus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: commits outrage by members of the Athenian garrison [against townsmen of Oropus] Under the agreement with the Oropians, an Athenian garrison occupied Oropus. After an outrage by some members of the garrison, the Oropians demanded its removal, and the Athenians eventually withdrew it after plundering Oropus again.

l: agreement between the Athenians and Oropians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Agreement between the Athenians and Oropians provides for an Athenian garrison at Oropus and Oropian hostages held by the Athenians, following settlement by promises and gifts. If the Oropians bring further charges, the Athenians must withdraw the garrison and return the hostages.

l: outrage by members of the Athenian garrison, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Some members of the Athenian garrison insulted townsmen of Oropus. The Oropians cited this outrage when they demanded the return of their hostages and the removal of the garrison.

l: Menalcidas, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Menalcidas, a Lacedæmonian by birth, served first as General of the Achæans and later as General of the Lacedæmonians. He promised Callicrates half of the Oropian money for help securing Achaean assistance, received the bribe, and then deprived Callicrates of his share. When prosecuted, he bribed Diæus to obtain acquittal, later quarrelled bitterly with him before the Senate, and falsely described the Roman decision to the Lacedæmonians. Chosen against Diæus, he persuaded the Lacedæmonians to violate the truce, captured and sacked Iasus, and stirred renewed conflict with the Achæans. Accused by the citizens, he killed himself by poison. He is described as unscrupulous, treacherous, imprudent, and iniquitous.

l: promise of payment to Menalcidas, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: amounts_to ten talents [offered by the Oropians] The Oropians promised Menalcidas ten talents if he would make the Achæans help them. Menalcidas promised half of this money to Callicrates.

l: Oropian appeal for Achaean assistance, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_refused_by Achæans [because of friendship and respect for the Athenians] The Oropians appealed to the Achæans for help after the Athenians refused to return the hostages and remove the garrison. The Achæans initially refused, but the Oropians then offered Menalcidas ten talents, after which assistance was decided upon.

l: Roman decision to assist the Oropians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_carried_out_by Achæans [against the Athenians] The Roman Senate responded to the Oropians’ appeal by ordering the Sicyonians to impose a fine on the Athenians. It reduced the fine from 500 talents to 100 talents at the Athenians’ request.

l: Diæus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Diæus is an Achæan general and leader whose actions shape the Achæans’ conflict with the Lacedæmonians and Rome. He first supports Menalcidas after accepting three talents, seeks Menalcidas’s acquittal, and deceives the Achæans about the Roman Senate’s decisions concerning Sparta. As successor to Damocritus, he agrees to await Roman arbitrators after Metellus’s second message, while winning over towns near Sparta and placing Achæan garrisons there. After being summoned before Orestes and later succeeded by Critolaus, he is again appointed commander-in-chief. He manumits slaves and raises an Achæan and Arcadian army, but, despite knowing of Critolaus’s defeat, sends only 4,000 men to Megara. After the Achæans’ defeat, he flees toward Megalopolis rather than defend Corinth, kills his wife to prevent her capture, and dies by poison.

l: the Romans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Romans are a group whose Senate sends ambassadors and envoys from Rome to oversee affairs in Asia Minor and arbitrate the Spartan-Achæan dispute. Their leisurely journey lets Diæus, Menalcidas, and Critolaus deceive the sides; the commissioners return to Rome without obtaining a general meeting.

l: the jurisdiction of the Achæan League, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The jurisdiction of the Achæan League was disputed by the Lacedæmonians and the Achæans. Menalcidas falsely told the Lacedæmonians that Rome had removed them altogether from it.

l: war between the Achæans and the Lacedæmonians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: A war between the Achæans and Lacedæmonians arose from disputes over Lacedæmonian jurisdiction and Roman authority. Though the Lacedæmonians sought alternatives to fighting, the war resumed despite Roman orders to await arbitration, ending in their defeat, Achæan occupation of nearby towns, and Menalcidas's truce violation.

l: the Roman arbitration of the Spartan-Achæan dispute, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Roman Senate announced that it would send ambassadors to arbitrate the differences between the Lacedæmonians and Achæans. The arbitration was delayed because the ambassadors traveled from Rome slowly, allowing Diæus and Menalcidas to misrepresent the Senate's decision.

l: the Roman Senate's directive concerning Sparta, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: directs Lacedæmonians [to submit all but capital cases to the Achæan League] The Roman Senate's stated directive was that the Lacedæmonians should try all cases except capital cases before the Achæan League. Diæus falsely represented this as permission for the Achæans to pass sentence of death upon a Spartan, while Menalcidas falsely claimed that the Lacedæmonians had been removed from the League's jurisdiction altogether.

l: Damocritus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Damocritus, General of the Achæans, defeated the Lacedæmonians but halted pursuit, choosing raids and plundering over siege. Fined 50 talents as a traitor for failing to follow up victory, he could not pay and fled the Peloponnese.

l: Macedonia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_to_be_settled_by Metellus [along with Achaia] Metellus brought his army from Macedonia and marched through Thessaly toward the Lamiac Gulf. Metellus wished to settle Macedonia and Achaia himself.

l: Laconia, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Laconia was overrun and plundered throughout by the Theban allies.

l: battle between the Achæans and the Lacedæmonians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: has_casualties about 1,000 Lacedæmonians [men in their prime in age and bravery] The battle ended in an Achæan victory, with about 1,000 Lacedæmonians in their prime killed and the rest fleeing into Sparta. Damocritus did not pursue the fugitives to the walls.

l: Achaean army, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_commanded_by Damocritus [during the campaign against Sparta] The Achaean army marched against Lacedæmon and defeated the Lacedæmonians. It was recalled from pursuing the fleeing enemy and then engaged mainly in raids and plundering rather than a regular siege.

l: Critolaus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Critolaus, son of Hicetaon, succeeded Diæus as General of the Achæans. Driven by an unreasoning desire to fight Rome, he deceived Roman envoys, gathered and commanded an Achæan army, and led it toward war against Sparta and Rome. Rejecting Metellus’ peace proclamation, he blockaded Heraclea, then fled toward Scarphea; after battle, he was neither seen alive nor found among the dead.

l: Tegea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Tegea is a district and town, called by poets the lot of Aphidas because Tegea and its neighbouring country were given to Aphidas. It received its name in the days of Tegeates, son of Lycaon. Its people were first distributed among eight parishes; Aphidas became a ninth during the reign of Aphidas. Aleus built the old temple of Athene Alea, made it the seat of his kingdom, and founded the town in its later form. Hippothous subsequently transferred the Arcadian kingdom’s seat from Tegea to Trapezus. The earlier temple of Athene Alea was destroyed by fire and rebuilt; Laodice sent it a robe from Cyprus. Tegea joined the Arcadians in war against Ilium, with the Persians, and at Dipæa, and repeatedly resisted the Lacedæmonians, including victories credited to its armed women and to snow weakening invaders. It dedicated offerings at Delphi from Lacedæmonian spoils and erected a statue of Philopœmen. Its temples, market-place, race-course, games, spring, festival, and statues mark its civic and religious life. Its boundaries and roads connect it with Megalopolis, Pallantium, the Lacedæmonian district, Thyrea, and Argos; the Alpheus marks one boundary and disappears into the plain of Tegea.

l: Amphissa, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Amphissa was a town about 120 stades from Delphi, the largest and most famous of the Ozolian Locrians. Its original inhabitants were Locrians; later, ashamed of the Ozolian title, they joined the Ætolians. Its notable sights were tombs of Amphissa and Andræmon and a citadel temple and statue of Athene, and it celebrated Anactes rites.

l: the Roman arbitration, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Roman arbitration held that several communities should not be compelled to remain in the Achæan League. Orestes and later Roman commissioners attempted to advance the settlement, but Critolaus obstructed the process and the commissioners returned to Rome.

l: the Lacedæmonian-Achæan disputes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Roman envoys were sent to settle the disputes between the Lacedæmonians and the Achæans. The negotiations broke down after the Achæans attacked Lacedæmonians at Corinth and Critolaus deceived the Roman commissioners.

l: the Achæan attack on the Spartans at Corinth, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_carried_out_by the Achæans [against Lacedæmonians residing at Corinth] After hearing the Roman decision, the Achæans attacked all Lacedæmonians residing at Corinth, identifying some by their hair, boots, dress, or names. They plundered suspected Lacedæmonians, dragged some from Orestes’ headquarters, and later imprisoned those they had arrested.

l: war between Rome and the Achæans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The war between Rome and the Achæans began when Critolaus gathered an Achæan army at Corinth and persuaded the Achæans to fight Sparta and the Romans, encouraged by Pytheas and the Thebans. The conflict brought ruin to Critolaus and the Achæans, ending in Roman victory, Corinth’s destruction, and punishment of opposing cities.

l: Mummius, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Mummius, a newly chosen consul and Roman commander, is ordered to lead naval and land forces against the Achæans, though Metellus hastens to finish the campaign first. Mummius then takes command, defeats the Achæans, captures and burns Corinth, kills or sells many inhabitants, removes treasures, punishes opposing cities, imposes fines, and establishes property-based chief-magistracies.

l: Heraclea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Heraclea is a city compelled into the Ætolian League, protected by the Ætolians after the Galati ravaged its country without taking it, then blockaded by Critolaus and the Achæans for refusing the Achæan League.

l: Mount Œta, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
