s: Mount Œta contains a narrow pass near Trachis and an easier route through Ænianes; Galati were defeated attempting one crossing, while Brennus used the other to reach the Greek force’s rear at Thermopylæ.

l: Elatea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Elatea is a town in Phocis, opposite Amphiclea and 180 stades away by road. Obscure before the Phocian War, it claims Arcadian ancestry and, according to the Elateans, was founded by Elatus. It was burned by Mede and shared the Phocians’ disasters, yet became next to Delphi the greatest town in Phocis. Its handsome market-place, temple of Asclepius, theatre with an ancient bronze Athene, and nearby temple of Athene Cranæa mark it. Elateans repulsed Cassander, resisted Taxilus and barbarians from Pontus, received Roman freedom and immunity, remained faithful to Philip, and were later reduced by Roman blockade.

l: Miltiades, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Miltiades, Cimon’s son and Athens’ chief magistrate, became Greece’s first public benefactor by defeating barbarians at Marathon and checking the Persian host.

l: Alcamenes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: commands 4,000 men [sent to garrison Megara and stop the Romans] Alcamenes was placed in command of 4,000 men sent to garrison Megara and stop Metellus’ advance. When the Roman army approached, he and his men panicked and fled without fighting to Corinth.

l: Megara, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_delivered_to Romans [without resistance] Alcamenes and his men were sent to Megara to garrison it and halt Metellus. They fled to Corinth when the Roman army arrived, and the Megarians surrendered the town without a fight.

l: Roman army, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: wins_battle battle near Scarphea [against Critolaus and the Achæans] The Roman army under Metellus defeated Critolaus’ forces near Scarphea, defeated the Arcadians at Chæronea, advanced to Thebes, and then marched on Megara. It did not burn Theban temples, destroy buildings, or attack fugitives other than Pytheas.

l: campaign against the Achæans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Romans ordered Mummius to conduct the campaign with naval and land forces, while Metellus hurried to complete it first. Metellus’ forces defeated the Achæans and their allies near Scarphea and Chæronea, occupied Thebes and Megara, and advanced to the Isthmus.

l: Metellus’ proclamation, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Metellus’ proclamation urged Lacedæmonians and other named cities to leave the Achæan League, promised no Roman anger for earlier disobedience, and later invited the Achæans to peace and harmony.

l: battle near Scarphea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Metellus’ army caught Critolaus and the Achæans during their retreat shortly before Scarphea. Many were killed and about 1,000 were captured, while Critolaus disappeared.

l: battle of Chæronea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The battle of Chæronea was a battle and fatal reverse for the Greeks, with Philip victorious; it fell most heavily on the Thebans. Phocians participated after Athenians and Thebans helped restore their towns. Afterwards Philip placed a Macedonian garrison in Thebes and restored the Platæans; Romans also cut down 1,000 Arcadians returning from Elatea at Chæronea.

l: Marathon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The victory at Marathon and the spoil taken from Datis provided the basis for the Athenian treasuries at Delphi.

l: peace and harmony between Romans and Achæans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_invited_by Metellus [through his proclamation] At the Isthmus, Metellus invited the Achæans to peace and harmony because he wanted to settle Macedonia and Achaia himself. Diæus’ folly prevented this intention from succeeding.

l: Roman army, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Roman army under Mummius, based at the Isthmus, numbered 3,500 cavalry and 22,000 infantry; with Cretan bowmen and Attalus's troops, it defeated the Achæans.

l: battle between the Romans and Achæans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Achæans attacked the Roman army before Mummius began the battle, but their cavalry immediately fled before the Roman cavalry. Their infantry resisted the Roman wedge-like attack until 1,000 picked Roman infantry took them in the flank and turned the battle into a complete Achæan rout.

l: Sicyon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Sicyon had authority over Donussa, which was described as a town subject to Sicyon. The Sicyonians associated with Sicyon invaded the land of the Hyperesians and later destroyed Donussa.

l: Epaminondas, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Epaminondas was a Greek general and Theban leader, son of Polymnis, of illustrious descent though raised in poverty. He studied national education carefully and, in youth, was a pupil of Lysis the Tarentine. He was especially mild and completely self-controlled, and later served as Philopœmen’s model in character and military achievement. He rescued Pelopidas, confronted the Lacedæmonians during an embassy, vowed vengeance for the daughters of Scedasus, and led the decision to fight at Leuctra. After victory, he exposed the Lacedæmonians’ losses, expelled their inland garrisons and governors, put down decemvirates, and aided the recovery and freedom of Greece. He supported the Arcadians, restored Mantinea, stirred the colonization of Megalopolis, and sent 1,000 picked Thebans to defend it; he also turned to Messene’s colonization and was credited with restoring Messene. As Bœotarch, including beyond the lawful term, he marched against Sparta, routed Iphicrates near Lechæum, and was acquitted for exceeding his term. He commanded near Pylæ and defeated Lacedæmonians, Achæans, and Athenians. Mortally wounded at Mantinea in victory, he watched the battle while holding his wound, then died and was buried on the field, commemorated by pillars and a dragon-bearing shield.

l: Roman Empire, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Roman Empire, through the elder Antonine, granted Pallantium privileges because of its association with Evander and the Arcadian settlement near the Tiber.

l: Augustus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Augustus is a Roman emperor whose actions reshape cities, populations, political representation, and sacred objects after victory over Antony and his allies. Near Actium, he populates Nicopolis with Ætolians, relocates people to fill it, transfers statues from Ætolia and Acarnania there, and secures it a place in the Amphictyonic Council by moving votes from joined peoples and the extinct Dolopes. In Achæa, he enlarges Patræ by incorporating people from various towns, razes Rhypæ, and grants Patræ freedom and privileges. After his victory, he carries off the statue of Athene Alea and the Calydonian boar’s tusks, following an established custom, and displays the statue in his Forum at Rome.

l: Œbotas, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Œbotas, son of Œnias and a native of Dyme, won the foot race at the 6th Olympiad, first among the Achæans. Denied reward, he cursed them against Olympic victories. After consultation and honors, Sostratus won; thereafter Achæans sacrificed to Œbotas and crowned his statue when victorious.

l: Mother of the Gods, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: A goddess represented by statues, one gold with hippopotamus-tooth head, one small beside Apollo, and one taken from Proconnesus, whose temple has only pillars; as Dindymene Mother, she is honored at Patrae in stone.

l: Attes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Attes is a mysterious figure associated with the temple of the Dindymene Mother at Dyme and honoured by Lydia after celebrating her rites. His identity remains uncertain: traditions make him Calaus’s son, incapable of procreation, or Sangarius’s grandson, goat-raised and self-mutilated after Agdistis disrupted a wedding.

l: Olympic victory, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Œbotas was the first Achæan to win an Olympic victory, taking the foot race at the 6th Olympiad. After the Achæans honored him in response to his imprecation, Sostratus of Pellene won the boys’ race.

l: temple of the Dindymene Mother, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Temple in lower Patræ, Pindar’s votive offering, honours Attes and opens only one day each year.

l: Aroe, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Aroe is a town, named for tilling the soil and built by Eumelus under Triptolemus’s instruction in sowing corn. Its Ionians shared Artemis Triclaria’s grove and temple; Eurypylus landed nearby during a sacrifice, and Patreus later enclosed it within Patræ.

l: Anthea, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Anthea, a town built by Triptolemus and Eumelus and named for Antheas, was barred to Achaeans by Patreus; its inhabitants were later scattered.

l: Mesatis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Mesatis, a city between Anthea and Aroe, was linked to Dionysus’ rearing and danger from the Titans; Patreus barred Achæan settlement, and its inhabitants were later scattered after Patræ’s reverses.

l: Pelias, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Pelias, son of Æginetus and father of daughters, was targeted by Medea at Iolcos; his daughters dismembered and boiled him, leaving little for burial.

l: Nicopolis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: has_council_members six [in the Amphictyonic Council] Nicopolis near Actium was admitted to the Amphictyonic Council at the wish of Augustus. In the narrator’s time it supplied six members and sent delegates to every Amphictyonic Council.

l: Laphrian Artemis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: A goddess honored in the citadel of Patræ under a foreign title and statue, whose title was attributed to Laphrius or Artemis's lessened wrath against Calydon.

l: Calydon, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Calydon was once an inhabited place with priests of Dionysus; Coresus served there, and Callirhoe died at its harbour well, later named for her. It was later depopulated by Augustus to populate Nicopolis, while Patræ received its spoils.

l: statue of Laphrian Artemis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The statue of Laphrian Artemis, made of ivory and gold by Menæchmus and Soidas, depicts a huntress and was brought from Calydon to Patræ after Augustus depopulated Calydon.

l: Laphria, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Laphria is an annual festival held by the people of Patræ for Artemis. It begins with a splendid procession, ending with a virgin priestess riding in a chariot drawn by stags, and continues the following day with sacrificial rites burning live birds, animals, and tree fruit on a large altar.

l: Eurypylus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Eurypylus, son of Euæmon, receives a chest containing a statue of Dionysus after Ilium’s capture. Opening it drives him mad, though he sometimes recovers. Seeking Delphi’s oracle, he is told to dedicate the chest at a strange sacrifice. At Aroe the sacrifice stops and he recovers; afterward Patras annually sacrifices to him during Dionysus’s festival. He also kills Axion.

l: Comætho, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Comætho, Artemis Triclaria’s beautiful priestess, mutually loves Melanippus; their temple union provokes divine anger, bringing famine, sickness, and human sacrifice.

l: Melanippus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Melanippus, a Theban warrior of exceptional beauty and ability, deeply and mutually loved Comætho. Their violation of Artemis Triclaria's temple brought famine, sickness, mortality, and an oracle demanding annual human sacrifices. In the Argive siege of Thebes, he killed Tydeus and Mecisteus before Amphiaraus reportedly slew him.

l: Hephæstus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Hephæstus, called a son of Talos, is a maker credited with Zeus’s sceptre, Agamemnon’s sceptre, a brazen bowl, and a Troy-brought chest; Agamemnon’s sceptre is probably his only extant work. He also represents Linus’s song.

l: Cassandra, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: holds Athene [the wooden statue, after tearing it from its base] Cassandra is shown seated on the ground and holding fast to the wooden statue of Athene. She had torn the statue from its base when Ajax dragged her away from the altar.

l: Patras, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: keeps the festival of Dionysus [annually] The people of Patras record no Eurypylus other than Eurypylus son of Euæmon. They offer sacrifices to him every year during their festival of Dionysus.

l: Cirrha, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Cirrha, formerly called Crisa in Homer and the Hymn to Apollo and reportedly named after Nymph Cirrha, lay about 60 stades from Delphi. Its people impiously ravaged Apollo’s sacred land; the Amphictyones captured and punished them. It then became Delphi’s seaport, containing a temple of Apollo, Artemis, and Leto and statues.

l: the temple of Artemis Triclaria, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The temple of Artemis Triclaria became Comætho and Melanippus’s bridal-chamber after their love, provoking Artemis’s anger and annual human sacrifices.

l: the altar of Artemis Triclaria, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: A lad and maiden were being led to the altar of Artemis Triclaria when Eurypylus came ashore near Aroe. This sacrifice revealed to Eurypylus and the local people the place intended by the oracle at Delphi.

l: the river Amilichus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Formerly unnamed river near Artemis Triclaria, called Amilichus, “Relentless,” during annual human sacrifice because of the sacrifice.

l: Milichus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Milichus is a river near Patræ, named Mild after Eurypylus arrived and human sacrifice was stopped.

l: the chest containing the statue of Dionysus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: A chest containing a statue of Dionysus and Æsymnetes is said to have been made by Hephæstus and given by Zeus to Dardanus. After Ilium’s capture, Eurypylus received it; traditions say Æneas left it or Cassandra discarded it. Opening it drove Eurypylus mad, and a priest later carries it outside the temple during a festival night.

l: the statue of Dionysus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The statue of Dionysus, said to be made by Hephæstus and gifted by Zeus to Dardanus, was in Eurypylus’s chest after Ilium’s capture; its sight maddened him and its arrival ended sacrifice to Artemis Triclaria.

l: the annual human sacrifice to Artemis Triclaria, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: An annual sacrifice of the most handsome maiden and lad, instituted after an oracle blamed famine, sickness, and mortality on Comætho and Melanippus, continued until Eurypylus arrived and dedicated the chest containing Dionysus’s statue, ending it.

l: the capture of Ilium, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The capture of Ilium is represented in a painting in The Lounge, together with the Greeks’ preparations for their departure. The scene includes the Trojan women as dejected captives and shows events involving Helen, Æthra, Andromache, Polyxena, and others. The capture of Ilium is represented through scenes of Trojan deaths, the carrying out of Laomedon’s corpse, and the guarded household of Antenor. Simonides’ inscription says that Polygnotus painted these incidents.

l: love, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_a feeling [felt worth life by human beings] Love brought Comætho and Melanippus together despite opposition from their parents and led them to violate the temple of Artemis Triclaria. The text says that love can confound human laws and upset honor due to the gods, but that human beings regard love as worth life.

l: Æsymnetes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_a god Æsymnetes is the god inside the chest. Nine men and nine women, chosen by the people for their worth, look after his worship.

l: festival of Æsymnetes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: includes special night rites [one night during the festival] During one night of the festival, the priest takes the chest outside the temple and special rites are performed. The lads of the district go to the Milichus wearing crowns of corn, bathe in the river, put on crowns of ivy, and go to the temple of Æsymnetes.

l: grove of Laphrian Artemis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: contains temple of Athene Pan-Achæis The grove of Laphrian Artemis contains the temple of Athene called Pan-Achæis.

l: temple of Athene Pan-Achæis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: contains statue of Athene Pan-Achæis The temple of Athene Pan-Achæis stands inside the grove of Laphrian Artemis. Its statue of the goddess is made of ivory and gold.

l: market-place of Patræ, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The market-place of Patræ contains temples of Olympian Zeus, Hera, and Apollo, Athene's open-air statue, Patreus's tomb, an outlet gate with golden effigies, and the Odeum.

l: temple of Apollo, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: A temple of Apollo is a sacred place associated with Patrae and Delphi. At Patrae it stands in the market-place near a naked bronze Apollo and the tomb of Patreus. At Delphi it was plundered before Philip ended the war, after which the Phocians lost participation. Its vestibule bears sayings, and its contents include Homer, Poseidon, the Fates, Pindar’s chair, an altar linked to Neoptolemus, and gold Apollo statues.

l: statue of Apollo with his foot on an ox skull, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: A naked brass Apollo statue wears sandals and places one foot on an ox skull, an image inferred to reflect Apollo’s association with oxen.

l: Hermes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Hermes is a god, especially regarded by the people of Pheneus, who held Hermæa games and maintained a temple for him. According to Arcadian and local traditions, he was washed after birth by mountain nymphs at the wells of Tricrena, was brought up at Acacesius, and was believed to have been reared under purslane. He bears a title from Cyllen and is associated with Mount Cyllene, where a ruined temple held an eight-foot juniper-wood statue. At Chelydorea he found a tortoise, skinned it, and made a lyre from its shell; he later taught Amphion to play it and appears at Helicon contending with Apollo over a lyre. He is Zeus’s messenger, receives Zeus’s sceptre from Zeus, and conveys departed souls to Hades. Greek tradition makes him father of Myrtilus. His worship and images range from roadside, square, stone, and wooden statues to temples shared with the Muses and Apollo or formerly with Hercules. At Tanagra he was honored as Ram-carrier and Champion: he ended pestilence by carrying a ram around the walls, led the young men against the Eretrians, and chiefly caused the Euboeans’ rout using a scraper. At Pharæ, sacred fish, an oracle, a well, and thirty god-named stones accompanied his statue.

l: Troy, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_destroyed_by Paris [through his outrage against Menelaus] Troy is depicted as being attacked and destroyed: Epeus knocks down its walls, and the Wooden Horse appears above them. The painting also shows the slaughter of Trojan men.

l: Trojans, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: After Ilium’s capture, Trojans escaping with Æneas reach Sardinia, mix with Greeks, and flee to inaccessible mountains after the Greeks’ defeat by Libyans; their descendants are called Ilians. They are also shown suffering in Troy’s sack, as Neoptolemus kills Elasus and Astynous.

l: Odeum of Patræ, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The Odeum stands next to the market-place. It contains a notable Apollo statue made from spoils won when the people of Patræ alone among the Achæans aided the Ætolians against the Galati. Richly beautified, it is surpassed only by the larger, better-equipped Odeum at Athens.

l: Artemis Limnatis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: has_temple_near Tegea [about seven stades beyond the altars] Preugenes is said to have taken the statue of Artemis Limnatis from Sparta to Patræ. The goddess is celebrated in a festival during which the old statue is carried from Mesoa to the sacred precincts at Patræ.

l: grove and temple of Artemis Limnatis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_located_at Patrę [opposite the market-place at an outlet] The grove and temple of Artemis Limnatis lie opposite the market-place at an outlet of Patræ. The sacred precinct contains several temples approached by porticoes rather than standing in the open air, including temples of Æsculapius and Athene.

l: statue of Artemis Limnatis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_kept_at Mesoa [generally, because Preugenes originally took it there] The statue was taken from Sparta by Preugenes and is generally kept at Mesoa because it was originally taken there. During the festival of Artemis Limnatis, one of the goddess's servants carries the old statue from Mesoa to the sacred precincts at Patræ.

l: festival of Artemis Limnatis, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: includes transport of the statue of Artemis Limnatis [from Mesoa to the sacred precincts at Patræ] At the festival, one of the servants of Artemis Limnatis carries the old statue from Mesoa to the sacred precincts at Patræ. Preugenes and Patreus receive annual funereal rites at the same time.

l: Aphrodite, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Aphrodite is a deity worshipped through temples, sacred enclosures, and many statues across places including Patræ, Ægium, Golgi, Orchomenus, Psophis, near Tegea, and near Mount Eryx in Sicily. At Patræ she has harbour and seaside sanctuaries; its women are especially devoted to her, and her images include one fished up by fishermen and a wooden figure with stone fingers, toes, and head. Her sanctuary at Psophis is ruined, while the temple near Mount Eryx is described as ancient and wealthy. She can act directly: after Selemnus lost Argyra, she transformed him into a river and later gave him forgetfulness of Argyra. She obtains good matches for the daughters of Pandareus from Zeus and receives prayers from widows at Naupactus seeking a second husband. Called Inventive, she is associated with most inventions in word or deed. Her representations take varied forms and names: Celestial, Common, Pandemian, Heart-Turner, Black, and an untitled image; some are wood, some stone, marble, or mixed materials, and makers include Damophon, Euclides, and Praxiteles. Her temples can also preserve memory, as at Actium’s seafight.

l: Calydonians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Calydonians, inhabitants of Calydon, became insane and died after Coresus appealed to Dionysus; consulting Dodona, they learned the god’s wrath would persist until Callirhoe or a volunteer was sacrificed.

l: Callirhoe, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Callirhoe, loved but rejected by Coresus, is chosen as Calydon's victim; when Coresus dies for her, she repents and kills herself at a harbour well.

l: insanity of the Calydonians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_a divine_punishment [inflicted by Dionysus] The insanity of the Calydonians was caused by Dionysus after Coresus prayed to him. The Calydonians became insane as if drunk and died beside themselves, and the oracle at Dodona said the condition would not end until Callirhoe or another volunteer was sacrificed.

l: death of the Calydonians, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_caused_by insanity of the Calydonians The Calydonians died beside themselves after Dionysus caused them to become insane. Their deaths led them to consult the oracle at Dodona about the cause and remedy of the affliction.

l: Dodona, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Dodona is an oracle believed by mainland peoples to give responses from doves and an oak. Consulted by the Calydonians, it later conveyed Zeus’s instruction that Athenians respect and spare conquered Lacedæmonian suppliants.

l: oracle at Dodona, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The oracle at Dodona attributes the Calydonians’ affliction to Dionysus and requires Callirhoe’s sacrifice or a volunteer’s death to end it. Later it exhorts Athenians to respect suppliants, commands mercy toward conquered Lacedæmonians, and instructs the Athenians to colonize Sicily.

l: sacrifice of Callirhoe, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: A required sacrifice prescribed to end Dionysus's wrath and Calydonian affliction: after preliminary rites, Callirhoe is led to the altar, but Coresus kills himself instead.

l: self-sacrifice of Coresus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: is_a substitute sacrifice [performed instead of Callirhoe] The self-sacrifice of Coresus occurred when he served as priest at the altar and killed himself instead of Callirhoe. He acted from love rather than anger, and Callirhoe repented after seeing him dead.

l: suicide of Callirhoe, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: occurs_at Callirhoe spring [at the well in Calydon near the harbour] Callirhoe's suicide followed Coresus's death in her place. Moved by pity and shame at his fate, she cut her own throat at a well in Calydon, which was thereafter called Callirhoe.

l: Menelaus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Menelaus musters an army against Troy, comes to Caphyæ, and plants a plane-tree beside a well. At Aulis, a dragon omen appears during sacrifice and is later shown on his shield. After the capture of Ilium, he delays sailing with Nestor near Sunium to perform funeral rites for Phrontis, his pilot. His and Odysseus’s affection for Antenor’s family is said to have helped spare Laodice.

l: Demeter, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Demeter is a deity represented in temples, groves, mysteries, paintings, and several stone statues. At the precinct of the Great Goddesses, her stone statue is about fifteen feet high, with a small Hercules beside it and smaller statues of Demeter and Proserpine before a grove; another statue is visible only to the chest. She has temples at Copæ, of Demeter Thesmophorus, and of Demeter of the Marsh. Phigalian people say she gave birth to Despoena. After anger toward Poseidon and grief over Proserpine’s rape, she wore black and hid for a long time in a cave on Elaion, causing the earth’s fruits to fail until the Fates persuaded her to relent. She is also linked to Cabirian and Thasian mysteries.

l: Proserpine, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Proserpine is Demeter’s daughter, called Preserver by the Arcadians. She has a sea-shore temple at Ægium beside Poseidon’s, and statues including a 15-foot figure with wooden parts beneath its dress. Not celebrated by Pindar’s hymn before the dream, she is abducted while gathering flowers. Later, with Hercyna, she lifts a cave stone, causing water to burst forth and the river to be called Hercyna.

l: Earth, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Earth, seated in the temple of Demeter and represented by a very ancient statue, first possesses the oracle at Delphi, appoints Daphnis priestess, shares it with Poseidon, gives her share to Themis, and ultimately it passes to Apollo.

l: market-place of Pharæ, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The market-place of Pharæ has a large ancient circuit; at its center stand Hermes of the Market-place and a hearth for sacrifices and oracle consultation.

l: statue of Hermes of the Market-place, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Hermes of the Market-place is a small, bearded, square stone statue lying on the ground in the market-place of Pharæ, dedicated by the Messenian Simylus according to its inscription.

l: oracle of Hermes, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: The oracle of Hermes is consulted at evening near the statue of Hermes of the Market-place. A person burns frankincense, lights brazen lamps, lays a brass coin on the altar, whispers a question into the statue’s ear, then takes the next heard sound as the response.

l: Selemnus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Selemnus is a river near Argyra flowing into the sea, transformed by Aphrodite from a love-stricken figure and granted forgetfulness; its water cures love.

l: Selemnus (handsome youth), Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Selemnus, a handsome youth who fed flocks near Argyra, was loved by the sea-nymph until she stopped visiting after he lost his good looks.

l: Argyra (sea-nymph), Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Argyra, a sea-nymph, loved and slept with Selemnus after rising from the sea, then stopped visiting when he lost his good looks.

l: Alpheus, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Alpheus is a river whose course is described through repeated meetings, disappearances, and reappearances. It is said to rise at Carnasium, where Malus and Scyrus join it, and also to rise at Phylace, receiving a stream at the Meeting of the Waters. Near Asea it joins Eurotas, runs with it for about 20 stades, vanishes into a cavity, and emerges at Pegæ in Megalopolis; another account has it lost in the plain of Tegea, reappearing at Asea, then lost again and emerging at Wells. It receives Buphagus, Helisson, and Gatheatas, flows by Pisa and Olympia, passes beyond Cyllene into the sea, and is said to reappear at Ortygia in Syracuse, where it mixes with Arethusa.

l: love-cure, Pausanias' Description of Greece, Volume II
s: Love-cure is a traditionally believed water treatment: bathing in the Selemnus makes men and women forget love, a remedy the narrator says would surpass great wealth if true.
